questions.question: Astronauts float in the space station, so a student concludes 'there is no gravity up there.' The station orbits at ~400 km where g ≈ 8.7 m/s². Resolve the paradox: strong gravity, yet weightlessness?
questions.solution: Weightlessness is not zero gravity — it is zero SUPPORT force. Both the station and the astronaut fall around Earth together at the same rate (free fall in orbit), so the floor never pushes on the astronaut's feet: no normal reaction, no sensation of weight. Your scale reads the normal force, not gravity itself. The same happens momentarily in a broken elevator cable or a stomach-drop on a swing — gravity still acts fully; what vanishes is the floor pushing back.

questions.question: Going down a deep mine, does gravity increase (more Earth above pulling down?) or decrease? Derive the trend for uniform density.
questions.solution: It DECREASES, linearly to zero at the centre. At depth d (radius r = R−d), only the inner sphere of radius r pulls you (the outer shell's pull cancels by symmetry — Newton's shell theorem). That inner mass is M(r) = M(r/R)³, so g(r) = GM(r)/r² = (GM/R³)r = g·r/R — proportional to r. The 'extra Earth above' contributes nothing net: for every lump pulling you up there is a matching lump the other side. At the centre r = 0, pulls balance perfectly: g = 0.

questions.question: A 60 kg astronaut travels to the Moon (g = 1.6 m/s²). What is conserved — mass or weight? Give both values on each body.
questions.solution: MASS is conserved (60 kg everywhere) — it counts the astronaut's matter and sets inertia. WEIGHT changes: W = mg. Earth: 60 × 10 = 600 N. Moon: 60 × 1.6 = 96 N. In deep space (g ≈ 0): ~0 N, yet pushing the astronaut still needs the same force to accelerate (inertia!). Mass resists acceleration; weight is gravity's pull on that mass. Confusing them is why 'weight in kg' on bathroom scales is technically sloppy — scales show mass by assuming Earth's g.

questions.question: Why must a geostationary satellite sit over the equator at ~36,000 km — why can't it hover over Nepal at a lower height?
questions.solution: Two constraints. (1) Period: geostationary means period = 24 h (matching Earth's spin). From T² ∝ r³, only ONE radius gives 24 h: r ≈ 42,000 km from centre (~36,000 km altitude). Lower height = shorter period (LEO satellites lap Earth in ~90 min) — it cannot hover. (2) Plane: uniform circular motion needs the centre of the circle at Earth's centre; a circle 'over Nepal' at constant latitude is not centred on Earth, so gravity (always toward Earth's centre) cannot supply its centripetal force. Only the equatorial plane works.

questions.question: Doubling the distance between two masses reduces the force to one quarter. Why does doubling the MASS not have a comparable effect on distance's influence?
questions.solution: F = Gm₁m₂/r²: mass appears to the FIRST power while distance is SQUARED. Doubling a mass doubles the force; doubling distance divides it by four. Distance is the dominant lever in gravitation — which is why orbits are so sensitive to altitude and why surface gravity changes so little across a planet's mass range.

questions.question: Why is the gravitational field zero everywhere inside a hollow uniform spherical shell?
questions.solution: For any interior point, the shell can be divided into opposite patches whose masses go as (area) ∝ r² and whose attractions go as m/d². Since the patch area grows as distance squared while the pull falls as distance squared, the two contributions cancel exactly. Every pair cancels, so the net field is zero — Newton's shell theorem.

questions.question: An astronaut in orbit floats. Is gravity absent there? Explain why the answer is no.
questions.solution: At the ISS's altitude g is still ~8.7 m/s², barely less than at the surface. The astronaut and station are BOTH in free fall around the Earth with the same centripetal acceleration, so there is no normal force between astronaut and floor — the sensation of weightlessness. Floating means falling together, not zero gravity.

questions.question: A bag of rice weighs slightly more at the poles than at the equator. Give the two independent reasons.
questions.solution: (1) Earth is an OBLATE spheroid: polar radius is ~21 km shorter, and g = GM/r² grows as r shrinks. (2) Earth ROTATES: at the equator some of the gravitational pull must supply centripetal acceleration (ω²r), and the effective weight g_eff = g − ω²R is reduced; at the poles there is no rotational radius, so nothing is subtracted. Shape and rotation together make equatorial g about 0.5% lower.
